chapters.title: Chapter 21 · The Widow's Thanks
chapters.artPrompt: a warm sitting room with a fire, an elegant widow in black thanking a ragged boy who blushes and studies the floor, an old white-haired Welshman beaming beside them, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The Widow Douglas came to the Welshman's house that very day. She wished to see the boy who had saved her. When Huck was brought in, ragged and shy, she took both his hands. “So it was you,” she said softly. “You risked your life for me, and you never told me your name.” Huck studied the floor. “It wasn't anything much,” he mumbled. “Anyone would have done it.” But his ears were red with pleasure.
The widow thanks Huck, who studies the floor and turns red.

“It was everything,” said the widow. “And I know why you hid your name. You feared that man would harm you. But he has fled the town, and you are safe now. I shall not forget you, Huck. When I can do something for you, I will do it gladly.” The Welshman's eyes twinkled, for he was proud of his part in the night's work. The widow thanked him too, and his brave sons.
New word: gratitude - the warm wish to thank and repay a person who has been good to you.

There was more news that morning. Becky Thatcher had come home from her long visit, and St. Petersburg was gay again. There was to be a grand picnic on the ferryboat, with ice cream and cakes. After the landing, all the children were to visit McDougal's Cave with candles. Every boy and girl in town was invited, and everybody counted the days. There would be boats enough to carry the whole town. Tom heard the news and walked on air for the rest of the day.

Only one small cloud hung over Tom's happiness. Injun Joe had not been caught. He had fled into the night, and the hills had swallowed him. Somewhere the half-breed was still alive, and still remembering. But summer was shining, and Becky was home. Tom pushed the dark thought away and went to find his best clothes. He even brushed his hair without being told. It was good to be young in St. Petersburg that week.

chapters.title: Chapter 22 · The Picnic Begins
chapters.artPrompt: a gay ferryboat full of children in summer clothes sailing on a wide river, baskets of cakes and lemonade on deck, a village and green hills sliding past, bright morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The picnic morning came at last, blue and gold. The ferryboat was hung with flags, and the children poured aboard with their baskets. Ice cream and lemonade waited on the deck. Tom stayed close to Becky all the way up the river, and Becky was kind to him all the way. Judge Thatcher gave the word, and the boat pushed off from the shore. St. Petersburg waved goodbye from the bank.
The picnic ferryboat goes up the river, hung with flags and full of children.

Under the hill the children landed and ran shouting through the woods. Then came the ice cream, more than a village child sees in a year. The ice cream was half gone before the ladies could count the plates. Nobody could remember being so happy. In the afternoon somebody said the great word: the cave. McDougal's Cave lay under the hill, a labyrinth of stone passages miles long. The children took candles and streamed in at the great arched door, laughing at their own echoes.
New word: labyrinth - a maze of winding paths, where a person can easily lose the way.

Inside, the candles made little stars in the blackness. Stalactites hung from the roofs like stone icicles. Passages branched on every side, up and down, this way and that. The bigger children led, and the smaller ones held hands. Presently Tom and Becky slipped away from the others. “Let's find a new passage,” said Tom. “Nobody knows all the turns of this cave.” Becky agreed, as she always did on adventures. At each turn Tom marked a cross of smoke on the rock, so they could find their way back. At least, so he thought.

They passed a frozen waterfall of stone and a lake still as glass. Every new wonder pulled them one turn farther. Behind them the party's calling grew fainter, and fainter, and stopped. Tom and Becky laughed at the echoes and did not notice. The great cave had quietly closed its stone arms around them.

chapters.title: Chapter 23 · Deeper and Deeper
chapters.artPrompt: a boy and a girl alone in a stone passage underground, holding one small candle whose flame is the only light in the huge dark, blank rock walls around them, storybook illustration

blocks.text: After a while Becky began to count the turns. “Tom,” she said, “we ought to go back now. The others will be waiting.” “Oh, just one more wonder,” said Tom. But one wonder led to another, and the way back grew long. Presently Becky stopped. “Tom,” she said, in a very small voice, “I don't see any smoke marks.” Tom looked at the blank walls, and then at the candle. “We - we'll soon find one,” he said. But his heart had gone cold.
Tom and Becky hunt the walls for the smoke marks that are no longer there.

They hurried from passage to passage, hunting for a mark. Every wall was blank stone. Tom shouted, and only his own echo answered, turning his voice into strange laughter. “Let's not shout any more,” said Becky, catching his hand. “It sounds like ghosts.” They walked on. The great cave was silent now, and cold. The candle burned smaller and smaller. Once they heard water dripping, like a slow clock. Their little light was going, and they knew it.
New word: echo - a sound that bounces back from walls or hills, like a voice answering itself.

Then the flame fluttered and sank. Tom lit the last scrap of candle he had saved, and it burned a little while, and went out too. The darkness came down on them like a blanket. Becky cried, and Tom put his arms around her. They had a little cake saved from the picnic, and they ate half and kept half. Then they slept on the cold stone, worn out. Night and day became the same black thing.

Far above them the ferryboat sailed for home, gay with flags. Only at suppertime did the town learn that two children were missing. Then the joy went out of St. Petersburg. All that night, and for days after, men and women hunted the cave. They cried the children's names into the dark. For three days cannon had been fired above the cave, hoping the children would hear. But the hill was miles deep, and its passages did not give them back.

chapters.title: Chapter 24 · The Kite String
chapters.artPrompt: a boy crawling alone in a narrow stone tunnel holding a long kite string that trails behind him, a weak candle in his other hand, a girl waiting by a spring in a shadowy chamber beyond, storybook illustration

blocks.text: When Tom woke, hunger was gnawing at him. But he had one hope left: a kite string in his pocket, and a plan in his head. “You stay here by the spring, Becky,” he said. “I will creep along the passages and follow the string. Then I cannot get lost. If I find a way out, I'll come back for you.” Becky held his hand tightly. “You will come back,” she said. “Promise me.” “I promise,” said Tom. And he crawled away into the dark.
Tom crawls into the black tunnels, holding the kite string that leads back to Becky.

Tom crept on and on, feeling with his hands, the string paying out behind him. Passage after passage, turning after turning. At last, in a side tunnel, he saw a hand. A hand holding a candle, with an arm behind it. Tom's heart stood still. Then the whole figure stepped into view, and it was Injun Joe. Tom shrieked with all his might. Injun Joe fled as if the cave itself were chasing him. His footsteps died away. Tom fled too, back along the string, to Becky.
Talk together: Tom decides not to tell Becky about the hand with the candle. Why does he keep this fright to himself?

“Did you find the way out?” Becky asked. “Not yet,” said Tom. “It's a big cave. I shouted, to hear how big it was.” He could not tell her about the hand. They ate the last of the cake. Tom made the halves as unequal as he dared, and gave Becky the big one. Then he took the string and tried again, and again, until his knees would hardly carry him.

He rested, and held Becky's hand, and said the searchers would come soon. Far away in the town, hope was almost dead. People had begun to whisper sad words about the two lost children. But Tom Sawyer had not given up. He was saving his last strength for one more try. His lips were cracked, and his feet were sore.

chapters.title: Chapter 25 · The Star of Daylight
chapters.artPrompt: a thin boy lying flat at the mouth of a tiny hole in a rock wall, reaching toward a dazzling spot of sunlight beyond, a wide river and open sky visible through the hole, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Once more Tom went out on his hands and knees, with the string almost at its end. He was faint, and the dark pressed on his eyes like a weight. Then he saw it: a speck of daylight, far away, like a star in the blackness. Tom crept toward it, hardly breathing. At the end of the tunnel was a little hole in the rock. He put his face to it and saw the great river rolling in the sunshine. He shouted until his throat was raw. Then he went back for Becky.
Tom reaches the little hole, and beyond it the river and the shining sky.

“Come, Becky,” he said. “We are saved, and it is only a little way.” It was a hard way, but hope gave them new strength. Tom helped Becky up through the little hole. They came out upon a bluff above the river, blinking in the sun. They had wandered five miles from the great door of the cave. The men in a passing boat would hardly believe their story. But they took the children aboard and rowed for home.
New word: rescue - to set a person free from danger. The men in the boat rescued Tom and Becky from the bluff.

The news ran through St. Petersburg faster than a boy could run. The church bells rang, and the town poured out of its houses in lantern light. Strangers hugged each other in the street. Three days and three nights the children had been under the hill. Now they were home, and the town cried for joy and would not go to bed. The ferryboat dressed herself in flags again.

Tom was put to bed, weak as water but happy. Aunt Polly cried over him, and scolded him, and kissed him, all in one breath. For some days Tom and Becky lay still and gathered back their strength. And the neighbors came to the door, day after day, just to hear them tell it. Visitors tiptoed, and spoke as if in church.

chapters.title: Chapter 26 · Behind the Iron Door
chapters.artPrompt: a vast cave entrance in a cliff shut by a great new iron door with heavy bolts, an old judge talking to a pale boy propped in a garden chair, morning light on the bluff, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Tom grew stronger every day, and visitors still came to hear the story. For a week he had been the lion of the village. Every day he told it again, and every day it grew a little grander. The village paper told the whole story, and Tom read it over and over. Becky told her part to the girls. She always added, softly, how Tom had once taken her whipping at school. The two children walked in glory wherever they went.
Judge Thatcher tells Tom that the great iron door has been bolted - and Tom turns white.

One morning Judge Thatcher dropped in, beaming at Tom. “No child will ever be lost in that cave again,” he said. “That cave is a dangerous place for children. I have had the great door shut, and bolted, and locked with iron.” Tom sprang up in his chair. His face went white as paper. “Judge!” he cried. “Injun Joe is in the cave!” For a moment nobody in the room could speak a word. The judge went pale too.
Talk together: Tom feared Injun Joe, yet now he is frightened for him too. What is the difference between the two fears?

Within half an hour men were rowing for the cave with lanterns, and the judge went with them. All night St. Petersburg waited for news. Some pitied even Injun Joe, shut under the hill with no way out. Others remembered the graveyard, and said nothing. Tom lay awake a long time. He thought of a man alone in the blind dark, calling at a door that would not open. Tom knew that dark. He had walked in it himself. “Even Injun Joe,” he thought, “does not deserve three days of that.”

Tom was sorry for his old enemy, and that was to his honor. But the hill had already given its answer. The town held its breath, and the boats came back with long faces. When the searchers lifted the great bar at dawn, they found they had come too late.

chapters.title: Chapter 27 · The Death of Injun Joe
chapters.artPrompt: men with lanterns standing silent at a great iron door in a cave, a still figure lying at the foot of the threshold, one ray of lantern light on the stone floor, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The men lifted the bar and swung the iron door open. Their lanterns made a lane of gold in the dark. Just inside, at the foot of the threshold, Injun Joe lay still. In his last hour he had crept toward the light, as far as his strength would carry him. He died a hand's reach from the open air, and never knew it. The strongest man in the party turned away his face.
At the foot of the iron door the searchers find Injun Joe, still at last.

The news went down the river faster than the boats. St. Petersburg had lived in fear of that man for a year. Now the fear was gone forever. Yet the town could not quite rejoice. For the first time all summer, boys slept with their windows open. The reward notices came down from the walls that day. “I was afraid of him all my life,” Tom told Huck. “Now that it's over, I'm sorry for him. Being shut in that dark - I know what that is.”
Talk together: Tom helped catch Injun Joe, and yet he pities him now. What does that tell you about Tom?

Injun Joe was buried near the mouth of the cave. People came from miles around, in wagons and boats, almost as to a holiday. Even the children stopped their games to watch the earth fall. But Tom stood apart at the graveside, thinking. Words he had heard in the haunted house kept knocking at his mind: Number Two, under the cross. The answer came as clearly as if the dead man had spoken it.

“Number Two was his den,” said Tom, half to himself. “But he never slept there all the time we watched. And under the cross - Huck, I saw him in this cave. He was far from the door, with a candle in his hand.” Huck's eyes grew wide as saucers. “Tom,” he breathed, “you don't think - ” “I do think,” said Tom. “The treasure is in the cave.”

chapters.title: Chapter 28 · The Secret Under the Cross
chapters.artPrompt: two boys with a candle before a limestone wall inside a cave, gazing up at a great cross marked in candle smoke on the rock, their faces lit from below, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Tom's plan was simple. He and Huck would row a skiff to the little hole in the bluff. It was the same hole that had saved Tom's life. The treasure, if it was anywhere, was nearer to that hole than to the great door. Nobody would see them enter, and nobody would ask questions. “If we find it, it is ours,” said Tom. “We saw it first.” So the partners set off down the river, with candles, a knife, and a bag for the gold.
Tom leads Huck through the little hole and into the cave, hunting the cross.

Tom knew every turning of his own escape, and he led Huck along it by candle light. They passed the frozen waterfall and the still lake. Huck's teeth chattered at every corner, but he did not turn back. At last Tom stopped at a great rock in a wide passage. “Look,” he said, and held up the candle. There, on the face of the rock, a cross was drawn in smoke.
New word: cross - the shape of two lines meeting in the middle. Injun Joe had drawn his in candle smoke.

“It's a ghost's sign,” whispered Huck, going pale. “No ghost did this,” said Tom. “Ghosts don't smoke candles. A man drew that cross, and a man buried something under it. Dig here.” Tom dug with his knife, and then with a flat piece of board. Huck dug with his hands. The earth came up soft and easy, as if it had been opened before. Not two feet down, they struck wood.

The wood was a rude flooring laid over a hole in the rock. Under the boards lay a little chamber in the stone, and there sat the strong box of the haunted house. The boys looked at it a long moment, afraid to touch it, in case it should melt away. “It's found,” whispered Tom at last. “Huck, it's found!” They filled their bag with gold, coin by coin, and staggered back toward the daylight.

chapters.title: Chapter 29 · A Golden Shower
chapters.artPrompt: a lamplit parlor full of astonished guests, a boy pouring a stream of gold coins from a heavy bag onto a table, coins catching the candlelight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The Widow Douglas was giving a party that evening for her friends. Lamps were lit from hall to parlor, and the best cake was set out. Aunt Polly was there, and the Thatchers, and half the town. Mr. Jones meant to tell the guests how Huck had saved her from the robbers. Tom and Huck came in late, tired and mysterious, carrying a heavy bag between them. “Set it by the door,” said Tom. “Wait for the word.”
At the widow's party, Tom pours a river of gold coins onto the table.

The Welshman told his story, and the guests marveled at Huck. The widow said she had already promised him a home and schooling. “Huck don't need it,” said Tom suddenly. “Huck's rich!” Everybody laughed at the joke. Tom turned to the door. “Fetch in the bag,” he said. The guests thought Tom was making a little speech. And the gold poured out upon the table, coin upon coin, in a shining river.
New word: reception - a grand evening party where guests are welcomed and thanked. The widow's reception turned into a treasure show.

Nobody laughed now. The guests crowded round, and the candlelight ran over the gold like water. “Is it real?” people whispered, over and over. The widow counted it with the judge, and the counting took a long time. “So much money in one heap,” said the judge, “so help me, I never saw.” It came to a little over twelve thousand dollars. Twelve thousand dollars, found by two boys in a cave. Some people pinched the coins to be sure of them. The table nearly bent under it. Such a sight had never been seen in St. Petersburg.

The money was carried to the bank the next morning, and the judge himself carried one corner of the bag. Half was Tom's and half was Huck's, for they were partners, fair and true. Every soul in town talked of nothing else that night. Two boys of St. Petersburg, barefoot no longer, were rich beyond any farmer's dreams.

chapters.title: Chapter 30 · Tom's Golden Future
chapters.artPrompt: a village street where two boys walk side by side in new clothes while neighbors stare and point admiringly, an old judge clapping one boy's shoulder, warm afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: After that week Tom and Huck were famous in all the country round. People drove in from other towns just to look at them. The village paper printed the stories of their lives, as if they were generals. Even the barrel Huck used to sleep in was mentioned in the paper. Men went about digging under every haunted house in the county, hoping for another such find. The boys were pointed out wherever they went. It was a wonder their hats still fitted their heads.
Tom and Huck, the two famous boys, walk down the village street.

Judge Thatcher had taken a great liking to Tom. He had seen the boy under the ground, and he knew courage when he saw it. “That boy may be a great lawyer or a great soldier,” he said. “He has the two things that cannot be taught, sense and pluck. When he is ready, I shall help him to the best schooling in the land.” Becky's father shook Tom's hand whenever they met. Aunt Polly could hardly believe her ears.
Talk together: money made the boys famous, but courage made them loved. Which would you rather be praised for?

The two fortunes were put out at interest, safe in the bank. Each boy now had an income of about a dollar a day. It does not sound like much now. A grown man worked all week for eight dollars then. The boys could buy candy for the whole town if they pleased. Tom enjoyed every minute of his fame. He described the little hole so often he knew the speech by heart.

Huck stood at the edge of the crowds, and his face grew longer every day. For the widow's promise had not been forgotten. He was to live in a fine house now, with clean sheets, regular meals, and schooling. And a bath every Saturday, Huck said to himself. He looked at his freedom the way a boy looks at the last day of summer.

chapters.title: Chapter 31 · Huck's New Home
chapters.artPrompt: a scrubbed boy in stiff new clothes squirming on a parlor chair, a kind widow in black showing him a dinner table set with knives and forks, lamplight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The Widow Douglas took Huck into her home, as she had promised. He was washed, and combed, and dressed in good new clothes. A bed with sheets was found for him upstairs, all white and smooth. Huck stood in the fine parlor and hardly dared to breathe. “This is your home now,” said the widow kindly. “You shall be my son, and I shall take good care of you.” Huck had never heard such words in his life. He tried to thank her, and could not find the words.
Huck, clean and stiff in his new clothes, learns to live in the widow's fine house.

But a fine house has fine rules. Meals were served by the bell, and Huck must come when it rang, hungry or not. He must sit up straight, eat with a fork, and listen to a chapter of a good book every evening. He must wear shoes in the street and a collar on Sunday. Worst of all, he must go to school when summer ended. Huck bore it all for three weeks. Three weeks is a long time for a boy who has slept in barrels.
New word: patience - the power of bearing hard things quietly and without complaint. Huck needed a great deal of it.

Tom came by and found Huck sighing at the gate. “I can't stand it, Tom,” Huck whispered. “The widow is good to me, and she means well. They are all very kind, and that is the worst of it. But a body can't stand so much goodness all at once. And school is coming in the fall, Tom. School.” Tom laughed, but he was sorry too. He knew exactly how new shoes pinch, in every kind of way.

At night Huck lay between the clean sheets and listened for the sound of rain on barrels. There was none. The sheets were smooth, and the bed was soft, and it did not matter. He could not sleep in them, try as he might. “I slept better in the rain,” he told Tom mournfully.

chapters.title: Chapter 32 · Huck Runs Away
chapters.artPrompt: a ragged boy sitting contentedly in an empty wooden barrel behind a fence, his fine new clothes hung neatly on a nail nearby, morning light through the trees, storybook illustration

blocks.text: At the end of three weeks, Huck was gone. The widow sent people looking for him all day, and the police looked too. Tom looked as well, in all the old places. He had left his fine new clothes behind him, every stitch. On the second evening Tom found Huck in the old hogshead behind the slaughter-house, ragged and dirty, comfortable and free.
Tom finds Huck back in the old hogshead, ragged and free.

“Huck,” said Tom, “you have frightened the widow half to death.” “I couldn't help it,” said Huck. “The widow eats by a bell, Tom. She goes to bed by a bell. She gets up by a bell. Everything is so awful regular a body can't stand it. The sheets are white, and you have to keep them white. And the fork - Tom, there was a fork for every different thing on the table. And the towels. There was a fresh towel every single day.”
Talk together: the widow's rules are meant with love. Why do they still make Huck unhappy? What would you miss most about freedom?

“Well, everybody lives that way,” said Tom. “Rich people, I mean. That is what being rich is.” “Then I don't want to be rich any more,” said Huck. “I had my try at it. It don't suit me, and it ain't no use pretending. I'm different, Tom.” He pulled his rags about him with a proud little air. For once, Tom Sawyer had no answer ready.

“The woods are better for me,” said Huck. “I slept better in the rain, up among the barrels. The widow is good, I know it. But I had to wear shoes, and I couldn't smoke, and I had to say lessons. I tried, honest I did. Don't ask me to go back, Tom.” Tom looked at his friend, ragged and free, and fell silent. Freedom sat on him again like an old coat. A boy who cannot sleep in sheets is not a rich boy, whatever the bank says.

chapters.title: Chapter 33 · What Riches Are Worth
chapters.artPrompt: two boys sitting on empty barrels behind a wooden fence at dusk, one ragged and one in neat clothes, talking seriously, a rising moon over the trees, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Tom sat down on the edge of the hogshead and thought a while. “Tell me the worst of it,” he said at last. “Well,” said Huck, “I have to wash every day. The water was hot, Tom. Hot, every single morning. I have to sleep in a bed with sheets. I have to wear shoes on Sunday, and a collar the whole day long. It is all fine for people who like it. But I'm different, and it ain't no use trying. And school is coming, Tom. School, with a stool in the corner.”
Two boys sit on empty barrels behind a fence, talking over Huck's troubles.

“But everybody that is anybody lives that way,” said Tom. “It is what being rich means.” “Then being rich ain't what it's cracked up to be,” said Huck. “It's only worry and sweat, Tom. You worry about your money, and you sweat in your good clothes. A barrel and a pipe is worth more than a bank, if you ask me.” Tom laughed until he nearly fell off the barrel. It was the finest speech Huck had ever made.
Talk together: Huck says riches bring worry and sweat. What good things can money not buy?

But Tom had not come only to talk about riches. He had brought a plan with him, and now he played it. “Huck,” he said, “money is not the only thing in the world. How would you like to belong to a gang?” Huck looked up quickly. “A gang of what?” “Of robbers,” said Tom grandly, “as fine a band as ever rode. Every boy in town will envy you.” Huck's eyes began to shine in the dusk. “Robbers!” he breathed. “Now you're talking. What do I have to do?”

“Ah,” said Tom, “that is the difficulty. That is exactly the difficulty.” And he looked slowly at Huck's rags, from the ragged hat to the bare feet, and shook his head. “What difficulty?” asked Huck, sitting up straight. “What rags? What's wrong with rags?”

chapters.title: Chapter 34 · The Robber Gang
chapters.artPrompt: a ragged boy and a neat boy shaking hands solemnly over an empty barrel by moonlight, as if signing a great contract, storybook illustration

blocks.text: “The difficulty is this,” said Tom. “We can't let you into the gang in rags. Nobody could. A robber has to be respectable, or the whole band is disgraced.” “No robbers in rags?” said Huck. “None that anybody respects,” said Tom. “A robber is more high-toned than a pirate, as a general thing. In most countries robbers are awful high up in the world - dukes and such.” “Dukes,” said Huck, considering. Even pirates looked up to a good robber, Tom added, warming to his subject.
Tom explains that even robbers must be respectable, and Huck begins to weaken.

Huck thought it over. Dukes were fine people, he had heard, with horses and castles and gold lace. “If I go back to the widow,” he said, “and stand the collar and the bell - can I join?” “You can,” said Tom. “It's a bargain, then,” said Huck. They shook hands on it, twice, to be sure. Then they built castles in the air together, with masks and horses and caverns.
New word: bargain - an agreement where each person gives something and gets something. Huck gave up his freedom; he got a robber band.

“And Tom,” said Huck, with a sudden fear, “you won't ever tell on me? About the widow's house, or anything?” “Tell on my own lieutenant?” cried Tom. “Not if they stretch my neck for it. Robbers never betray robbers. That is the first law of the band.” Huck was satisfied. Then he sighed. “The sheets are going to be the death of me, Tom.” “You'll get used to them,” said Tom. “Everything comes right, if you wait.”

“When does the gang start?” asked Huck. “When the time is ripe,” said Tom grandly. “A band like ours cannot be hurried. There are caves enough along this river for a hundred dens. We shall ride out one day, and St. Petersburg will tremble.” Huck believed every word of it. And so, as the crickets began to sing, the two friends struck the grandest bargain of the summer.

chapters.title: Chapter 35 · The End of a Boy's Story
chapters.artPrompt: two boys walking side by side along a river bank at dusk, one neat and one ragged, the lights of a village beginning to shine across the water, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The two friends walked back toward the widow's house as the stars came out. The frogs sang in the shallows, and the crickets sang in the long grass. A late boat went by with a red light. Huck walked slower and slower as the lamps came nearer. But a bargain was a bargain, and a robber never goes back on his word. At the gate Tom shook his hand once more. “Remember,” he said, “collars, and school, and the band.” Huck groaned, and went in.
Tom and Huck walk home together under the first stars.

And so ended the strangest summer any boy of St. Petersburg ever had. Tom had whitewashed a fence without lifting a brush, and gone to his own funeral. He had been a pirate, a hero, a witness, a detective, a lost child, and a finder of treasure. He was rich now, and famous, and Becky Thatcher smiled on him. Aunt Polly was proud of him at last. He still hated Sundays, and he still loved his freedom. What more could a boy want?
Talk together: which of Tom's adventures did you like best? What would you have done in his place?

But this is where the story must stop. It is the history of a boy, and it must end as a boy's story ends. Boys' stories end with the summer, and this one is no different. If it went any further, Tom would have to grow up. Then it would be the history of a man. And that, as Tom himself would tell you, is quite another kind of book.

The lamps of St. Petersburg shone on the great river, one by one. In the widow's house a boy lay between clean sheets, wide awake, thinking of masks and horses and buried gold. Somewhere out on the river a night bird called, and was answered. The whole town slept in peace, and the river went on singing. And Tom Sawyer walked home whistling under the stars.
